questions.stem: Improve: 'He insisted to go to the party alone.' Choose the grammatically correct version.

options.option_text: He insisted for going to the party alone. (wrong: 'insist for' is non-standard)
He insisted on going to the party alone. (correct: insist + ON + gerund is the standard construction ✓)
He insisted in going to the party alone. (wrong: 'insist in' is not standard)
He insisted about going to the party alone. (wrong: 'insist about' is non-standard)

questions.explanation: B is correct. INSIST + ON + gerund (-ing). 'Insisted to go' = wrong. 'Insisted on going' = correct. Fixed preposition with 'insist': always ON. Other gerund-requiring verbs: object TO, look forward TO, succeed IN, interested IN.

questions.stem: Improve: 'She is elder than her sister by two years.'

options.option_text: She is older than her sister by two years. (correct: 'elder' is used only for family members without 'than'; when 'than' is used, 'older' is required ✓)
She is eldest than her sister by two years. (wrong: eldest is superlative, not comparative)
She is more elder than her sister by two years. (wrong: double comparative)
The sentence is correct as is. (wrong: 'elder than' is incorrect in standard grammar)

questions.explanation: A is correct. ELDER/ELDEST: used without 'than' for family members. OLDER/OLDEST: comparative/superlative used with 'than.' 'My elder brother' (no 'than') ✓. 'She is OLDER than her sister' (with 'than') ✓. 'Elder than' is generally considered incorrect in formal grammar.

questions.stem: Improve: 'He is one of the best doctor in the city.'

options.option_text: He is one of the best doctors in the city. (correct: 'one of' must be followed by a plural noun ✓)
He is one of the better doctor in the city. (wrong: 'better' is comparative, 'best' is superlative which is needed)
He is one of the best doctor's in the city. (wrong: apostrophe incorrect; plural needed, not possessive)
He is one of the best doctor in the cities. (wrong: 'doctor' must be plural)

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'ONE OF THE + superlative + PLURAL NOUN.' This is a fixed construction. 'One of the best doctors' (plural noun after 'one of the best'). Verb after the entire phrase: singular (He IS one of...). Common error: using singular noun after 'one of the.'

questions.stem: Improve: 'I prefer tea more than coffee.'

options.option_text: I prefer tea over coffee. (acceptable but 'prefer...to' is the standard form)
I prefer tea to coffee. (correct: 'prefer A to B' is the standard construction; not 'prefer...more than' ✓)
I prefer tea rather than coffee. (also grammatically correct and widely used, but the 'prefer...to' form is more standard)
The original sentence is correct. (wrong: 'prefer...more than' is non-standard)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'PREFER A TO B' is the standard construction. 'Prefer tea MORE THAN coffee' is incorrect; 'than' is used in comparison, not with 'prefer.' Correct: 'I prefer tea TO coffee.' 'Prefer A rather than B' is also accepted in informal usage.

questions.stem: Improve: 'He was hanged for committing murder.'

options.option_text: He was hung for committing murder. (wrong: 'hung' is used for hanging objects; 'hanged' is the correct past tense for execution)
He was hanged for committing murder. (correct: 'hanged' = executed by hanging; 'hung' = suspended objects ✓)
He was hanging for committing murder. (wrong: 'was hanging' = past continuous, implies still ongoing)
He was made to hang for committing murder. (wrong: 'made to hang' is awkward and non-standard)

questions.explanation: B is correct. The original sentence is ALREADY CORRECT. HANGED = past tense of hang when referring to execution by hanging. HUNG = past tense for suspending objects ('He hung the picture'). 'He was hanged' = executed by hanging — correct. This is one of the most tested irregular verb distinctions.

questions.stem: Improve: 'The number of students are increasing every year.'

options.option_text: The number of students is increasing every year. (correct: 'The NUMBER of' = singular; takes singular verb ✓)
A number of students is increasing every year. (wrong: 'A number of' = several/many; takes plural verb 'are')
The number of student is increasing every year. (wrong: 'student' should be plural after 'number of')
The number of students were increasing every year. (wrong: 'were' = past plural; 'is' is needed)

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'THE NUMBER OF + plural noun' → singular verb. 'THE number IS increasing.' Compare: 'A NUMBER OF + plural noun' → plural verb. 'A number of students ARE absent.' This distinction (the number/a number) is one of the most tested SVA rules in SSC exams.

questions.stem: Improve: 'Hardly he had arrived when the phone rang.'

options.option_text: Hardly he arrived when the phone rang. (wrong: inversion required after 'Hardly' at the start)
Hardly had he arrived when the phone rang. (correct: negative adverb 'Hardly' at start → inversion: Had+he ✓)
Hardly he had arrived than the phone rang. (wrong: 'hardly...than' is incorrect; 'hardly...when' is correct)
He had hardly arrived when the phone rang. (also correct: inversion only required when 'Hardly' starts the sentence)

questions.explanation: B is correct. When 'HARDLY' begins a sentence, SUBJECT-AUXILIARY INVERSION is required: 'Hardly HAD he arrived...' not 'Hardly he had arrived.' Rule: negative/restrictive adverbs at sentence start (hardly, scarcely, no sooner, seldom, rarely, never) trigger inversion. 'He had hardly arrived' (no inversion when not at start) is also correct.

questions.stem: Improve: 'She is too weak to not walk.'

options.option_text: She is too weak to walk. (correct: 'too + adjective + to + infinitive' — the 'not' creates a double negative ✓)
She is so weak that she cannot walk. (also correct — alternative construction but not the 'improvement' of the given form)
She is too weak not to walk. (wrong: 'too weak not to walk' means she CANNOT avoid walking — different meaning)
She is very weak to walk. (wrong: 'very...to' is not standard; 'too...to' is the idiom for this meaning)

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'TOO + adjective + TO + infinitive' = so [adjective] that [subject] cannot [infinitive]. 'Too weak to walk' = so weak she cannot walk. Adding 'not' ('too weak to NOT walk') creates an illogical double negative. 'Too...to' already implies impossibility.

questions.stem: Improve: 'Between the two candidates, Priya is the most intelligent.'

options.option_text: Between the two candidates, Priya is more intelligent. (correct: superlative ('most') is for 3+; comparative ('more') for exactly 2 ✓)
Between the two candidates, Priya is the most intelligenter. (wrong: double superlative error)
Among the two candidates, Priya is the most intelligent. (wrong: 'among' = 3+; 'between' = 2; and 'most' still wrong for 2)
Between the two candidates, Priya is the more intelligent. (also correct: 'the more intelligent' = comparative with the article; both 'more intelligent' and 'the more intelligent' are accepted)

questions.explanation: A is correct. When comparing EXACTLY TWO items: use COMPARATIVE (more/er), not superlative (most/est). 'Between the two, Priya is MORE intelligent' ✓. 'Most intelligent' is for three or more. Also: BETWEEN = 2 persons; AMONG = 3 or more.

questions.stem: Improve: 'He said that he will attend the meeting.'

options.option_text: He said that he would attend the meeting. (correct: reported speech; main verb 'said' (past) → 'will' backshifts to 'would' ✓)
He said that he shall attend the meeting. (wrong: 'shall' backshifts to 'should', not 'will'; and 'shall' is formal for first person)
He told that he will attend the meeting. (wrong: 'told that' without an indirect object is incorrect; 'said that' is correct)
He said that he will have attend the meeting. (wrong: 'will have attend' is grammatically wrong)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Reported speech tense backshift: 'said' (past) → indirect speech tenses shift back. Direct: 'I WILL attend' → Indirect: 'he WOULD attend.' Will → Would in reported speech when the reporting verb is past. 'Said that he would attend' ✓.
